F(*xs) = {
    A = xs

    G(7, 8)

explanation: A transparent reference to a collecting parameter is that parameter's known slice: `A*` transfers the very cells `xs*` does, through any number of unbraced hops, so an unused failing argument is never evaluated and the second `tick()` still reads 1.

probes.source:
Inc(x) = x + 1
Apply(f) = f(9)
Pass(v) = {
    A = v
    Apply(A*)
}
Outer(*fs) = Pass(fs)
Outer(Inc)

explanation: The transferred cell keeps its CALLABLE channel: re-spreading a collected callable through a transparent reference hands it to `Apply` unforced, exactly as `fs*` does.
Transfer defers a failure to the operation that demands the cell, never suppresses it: a read of `ys` as a value materializes the collector, whose first element is the original division.

Written braces make a distinct carrier, and a calculation or a fixed parameter holding an ordinary computation is no collector: each is an arbitrary spread, evaluated during supply formation, whatever value it would have.

    A = xs

explanation: A transparent reference passed as one ordinary argument stays that one argument, and it keeps its way to the collector's original computations: the later explicit `v*` opens them unevaluated, exactly as with `Pass(xs)`, so the failing `1 / 0` is never demanded.

source:
Count(*ys) = ys.count
Pass(v) = Count(v), Count(v*)
F(*xs) = {
    A = xs
    Pass(A)
}
F(1 / 0, 2, 3)
explanation: Without a star the reference is one argument, however many elements the collector holds; only the explicit star opens its three positions.

Pass(v) = Apply(v*)
F(*xs) = {
    A = xs
    Pass(A)
}
F(Inc, 1 / 0)
explanation: The spread opens the original arguments, not their values, so the collected algorithm stays invocable and the unused failing element is never demanded.

F(*xs) = {
    A = xs
    Pass(A)
}
F(1 / 0)
explanation: The opened supply has a known count, so the wrong-arity call is rejected before the failing element could be demanded.

explanation: Written braces, a call and a fixed parameter holding an ordinary computation are computations, not references to a retained collector, so the spread evaluates them when it is formed; reading the collector as a whole value stays eager too.

source:
CountItems(*xs) = xs.count
CountItems(1 / 0)
explanation: A collecting parameter retains an exact slice of its argument computations. `count` reads that slice's length, one position per supplied argument, so it needs no element's value: the failing `1 / 0` is never demanded.
Postfix selection validates each position of a retained collector, then demands that one element. Positions 1 and 0 run; the third element is never selected, so its failure stays dormant.

source:
FirstItem(*xs) = xs[0]
FirstItem(10, 1 / 0)
explanation: Selecting position 0 needs only the first argument.

source:
Prefix(*xs) = xs.take(1)
Prefix(10, 1 / 0)
explanation: `take` validates its count, then demands exactly the kept prefix in source order and builds an ordinary eager list from those values.

source:
Prefix(*xs) = xs.take(2)
Prefix(10, 1 / 0)
explanation: A requested element is demanded: the second position belongs to the prefix, so its failure is the failure of `take`.

source:
F(*xs) = xs[1], xs[0], xs[1]
F(tick(), tick())
explanation: Selected positions decide first-demand order: position 1 runs first and draws 1, position 0 draws 2, and the repeated position 1 reuses its one completed outcome instead of running again.
A transparent reference reads the collector's own cell, so `A.count` and `Box.B[0]` observe the same retained slice as `xs.count` and `xs[0]`.

source:
F(*xs) = xs
F(1 / 0)
explanation: Reading the collector as a value still builds its whole exact list; only a qualified observer reads positions.
A written list is ordinary eager data, even when it holds a collector's items and its selection needs only one of them.
A brace carrier is a computed value, not a transparent reference, so `count` receives its whole value.

Selecting a member that is a transparent reference to a collecting parameter is that parameter's known slice too: `Box.A*` transfers the very cells `xs*` does, as `Y = Box.A` then `Y*` does. The receiver's own output is never read, even when it is the same collector.
The transferred cell keeps its CALLABLE channel through a member path, exactly as through a name.
A member path defers a failure to the operation that demands the cell, never suppresses it.

A selected member keeps its own kind: written braces, a calculation or a fixed parameter holding an ordinary computation is no known slice, and neither is a stacked star or a call of the member, even when it is passed as one ordinary argument and spread by the callee.

ApplyFirst(*fs) = map([1, 2], fs*)
ApplyFirst(Inc)

Inc(x) = x + 1
Ignore(*xs) = 1
Ignore(Inc)

Inc(x) = x + 1
Collect(*xs) = xs
Collect(Inc)

Inc(x) = x + 1
Apply(f) = f(9)
Fwd(*fs) = Apply(fs)
Fwd(Inc)

Inc(x) = x + 1
Apply(f) = f(9)
Fwd(*fs) = Apply([fs*]*)
Fwd(Inc)

Apply(f) = f(9)
Fwd(*fs) = Apply(fs*)
Fwd(5)

explanation: A collecting parameter keeps the arguments it receives exactly as they were supplied, and re-spreading it with `fs*` hands those same arguments on. A function passed through `Fwd` therefore reaches `Apply` still callable: `Fwd(Inc)` means `Apply(Inc)`, which is 10. Collecting evaluates nothing, so an unused collected function or failing calculation never runs. Reading the collector as a value (`xs`) builds its list, which evaluates every element, so a function that needs an argument reports its own error there. The collected list itself is a value, not a function, and a value never becomes callable by passing through a collector.
